book: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology, 4th ed. (Rizzo)
kicker: Lesson 17 of your course, built from Chapter 17 of your Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology textbook (Rizzo). Test practice uses checked answers, because there is no official key for this test.

steps.title: What respiration means
teach: Cells need a constant supply of oxygen, and cellular respiration produces carbon dioxide, which forms carbonic acid if it builds up. So it must be removed quickly.

The respiratory system (nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and lungs) exchanges gases between the air and the blood. The cardiovascular system carries them between the lungs and the cells. The two systems share this job equally.
Respiration here means the overall exchange of gases between the atmosphere, the blood and the cells, which is different from cellular respiration in Chapter 4.

act.prompt: Which system shares the job of supplying oxygen and removing carbon dioxide equally with the respiratory system?

options.label: Cardiovascular
options.feedback: Right. The blood carries the gases.

options.label: Urinary
options.feedback: The urinary system helps with pH, but not this job.

steps.title: The nose
teach: Air enters through the nostrils (external nares). The internal nose connects to the pharynx through two internal nares. The nasal septum divides the right and left cavities. The vestibules, just inside the nostrils, are lined with coarse hairs that filter large particles.

Three shelves, the superior, middle and inferior conchae (turbinates), form passageways called the superior, middle and inferior meatus. Olfactory receptors are in the membrane lining the superior meatus.
The lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells. It warms, moistens and filters air; detects smells; and provides resonating chambers for speech.

items.label: Connect the nose to the pharynx
Just inside the nostrils, lined with hairs

steps.title: The pharynx
teach: The pharynx (throat) is about 5 inches long and carries both air and food. It’s also a resonating chamber for speech.
The nasopharynx is the uppermost portion. It has four openings (two internal nares and two auditory tubes) and the pharyngeal tonsils.
The oropharynx has only one opening, the fauces, which connects with the mouth. It holds the palatine and lingual tonsils.
The laryngopharynx is the lowest part; it connects to the esophagus behind and the larynx in front.

act.prompt: Put the parts of the pharynx in order from top to bottom.

steps.title: The larynx
teach: The larynx (voice box) is a short passage connecting the pharynx with the trachea. Nine pieces of cartilage support it.

Three unpaired cartilages: the thyroid cartilage (largest; the Adam’s apple), the epiglottis (a leaf-shaped flap that covers the glottis when you swallow) and the cricoid cartilage (a ring that joins the trachea).
Three paired cartilages: the arytenoids (ladle-shaped; move the vocal cords), the corniculates (cone-shaped) and the cuneiforms (rod-shaped, in the fold connecting the epiglottis to the arytenoids).

steps.title: Making sound
teach: The larynx has two pairs of folds: the upper vestibular folds (false vocal cords) and the lower vocal folds (true vocal cords). The glottis is the space between the vocal cords.
Air from the lungs makes the vocal cords vibrate and produce sound. More air pressure makes a louder sound.
Pitch is controlled by tension on the true vocal cords: tighter cords vibrate faster, giving a higher pitch. Men’s cords are usually thicker and longer, so their voices are lower.

act.prompt: What controls each quality of the voice?

items.label: Tension on the true vocal cords

steps.title: The trachea
teach: The trachea (windpipe) is an air passage about 4.5 inches long. It lies in front of the esophagus and runs from the cricoid cartilage of the larynx to the fifth thoracic vertebra. It carries only air, not food.
Its lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, which produce mucus; the cilia sweep mucus and dust up to the throat.
16 to 20 C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage keep it open. The open part of the C faces the esophagus so it can expand when you swallow.
Smoking can turn the lining into stratified squamous epithelium without cilia, causing smoker’s cough.

act.prompt: Why are the tracheal cartilage rings C-shaped?

options.label: The solid part keeps the airway open; the open part lets the esophagus expand when swallowing
So food can pass through the trachea
options.feedback: Food goes down the esophagus, not the trachea.

options.label: To make sound
options.feedback: Sound comes from the vocal cords.

steps.title: The bronchial tree
teach: The trachea divides into right and left primary bronchi. The right one is shorter, wider and more vertical, so swallowed objects often lodge there.

Entering the lungs, the primary bronchi divide into secondary, or lobar, bronchi (one per lobe: three on the right, two on the left), then tertiary (segmental) bronchi, then bronchioles, then terminal bronchioles.
As the branches get smaller, cartilage disappears and smooth muscle increases.

steps.title: The lungs and pleura
teach: The lungs fill the pleural divisions of the thoracic cavity. The right lung has three lobes and is shorter (the liver sits below it); the left lung has two.
The parietal pleura lines the chest wall; the visceral pleura covers the lung. The pleural cavity between them holds lubricating fluid. Inflammation here is pleurisy.
Each lung segment is divided into lobules, wrapped in elastic connective tissue, each with a lymphatic vessel, an arteriole, a venule and bronchioles from a terminal bronchiole.

act.prompt: How many lobes does the right lung have?
act.explanation: The right lung has three lobes; the left lung has two.

steps.title: Alveoli and gas exchange
teach: Terminal bronchioles divide into respiratory bronchioles, which divide into 2 to 11 alveolar ducts (also called atria). Around them are alveoli and alveolar sacs.

An alveolus is a cup- or grape-shaped outpouching of epithelium on an elastic basement membrane, surrounded by capillaries. Gases cross the alveolar-capillary (respiratory) membrane by diffusion. The lungs have over 300 million alveoli, about 70 square meters of surface.
Alveolar cells (type II) secrete surfactant, which lowers surface tension so the alveoli don’t collapse. Premature babies without enough surfactant get respiratory distress syndrome.

steps.title: Breathing and the three processes of respiration
teach: Ventilation (breathing) moves air between the atmosphere and the lungs. External respiration is gas exchange between the lungs and blood. Internal respiration is gas exchange between the blood and body cells.
Inhaling: the dome-shaped diaphragm contracts and moves downward, and the external intercostals lift the ribs. The chest gets bigger, pressure drops and air rushes in.
Exhaling: the muscles relax, the chest gets smaller, pressure rises and air flows out. This is mainly passive; forced exhalation uses the internal intercostals.

steps.title: Partial pressures
teach: Each gas in air contributes part of the total pressure: its partial pressure. Air is 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide, so PO₂ is about 160 mm Hg.

Gases diffuse from high to low partial pressure. In the lungs, oxygen moves from alveolar air (104 mm Hg) into capillary blood (40 mm Hg), and carbon dioxide moves from blood (45 mm Hg) into alveolar air (40 mm Hg). In the tissues, the reverse happens.

act.prompt: Why does oxygen move from the alveoli into the blood?

options.label: Its partial pressure is higher in the alveoli (104) than in the blood (40)
options.feedback: Right. Gases diffuse from high to low partial pressure.

options.label: Carbon dioxide pushes it
options.feedback: Each gas follows its own pressure gradient.

steps.title: Lung volumes and capacities
teach: Functional residual capacity (FRC): the gas left in the lungs at the end of a normal tidal exhalation.
Inspiratory capacity: the most you can breathe in from the end of a resting exhalation.
Vital capacity: the maximum volume you can breathe out at the normal rate after a maximum breath in.
Total lung capacity: the volume of gas in the lungs at the end of a maximum breath in.

items.label: Gas left after a normal exhalation
Most you can inhale from resting exhalation
Most you can exhale after a maximum inhalation
All the gas in the lungs after a maximum inhalation

steps.title: Respiratory disorders
teach: Emphysema destroys the walls of the alveoli, reducing gas exchange. Bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchi. COPD includes emphysema, asthma and chronic bronchitis. Asthma narrows the airways with spasms and thick mucus.
Cystic fibrosis is inherited and affects the secretory cells of the lungs, making mucus very thick. Pneumoconiosis comes from inhaling asbestos, silica or coal dust and scars the lungs.

The common cold is caused by a rhinovirus; influenza by a myxovirus; tuberculosis by Mycobacterium tuberculosis; Legionnaire’s disease by Legionella. Others: pneumonia, laryngitis, pleurisy, atelectasis (collapsed lung), lung cancer, whooping cough and SIDS.

items.label: Inherited; affects the lungs’ secretory cells
Caused by asbestos, silica or coal dust

steps.title: Breathing and aging
teach: Respiratory muscles weaken and the chest wall stiffens. Lung tissue loses elasticity, and lung capacity can fall by almost 35% by the 70s. Cilia work less, so mucus builds up and infections like bronchitis and pneumonia become more likely. Light exercise helps.

act.prompt: Why are older adults more prone to respiratory infections, according to the textbook?

options.label: Ciliary action decreases, so mucus builds up

quiz.q: Olfactory receptors are located in the membrane that lines the _______________________ meatus.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says olfactory receptors are located in the membrane that lines the superior meatus. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The _____________ is a tubular passageway that extends from the cricoid cartilage of the larynx to the fifth thoracic vertebra.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the trachea extends from the cricoid cartilage of the larynx to the fifth thoracic vertebra. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: Patients with __________________ suffer from the destruction of the walls of the alveoli.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says emphysema is characterized by the destruction of the walls of the alveoli. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The __________________ residual capacity is the volume of gas in the lungs at the end of a normal tidal volume exhalation.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says functional residual capacity is the volume of gas in the lungs at the end of a normal tidal volume exhalation. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: In the lungs, the grapelike outpouchings of epithelium and elastic basement membrane surrounded externally by a capillary network are called __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 describes alveoli as grapelike outpouchings of epithelium and elastic basement membrane surrounded by a capillary network. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The uppermost portion of the pharynx is called the _______________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the uppermost portion of the pharynx is the nasopharynx. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The internal nose connects with the pharynx via two openings called the internal ___________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the internal nose connects with the pharynx via two openings called the internal nares. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: Each segment of lung tissue is divided into a number of _____________ wrapped in elastic connective tissue with a lymphatic, an arteriole, a venule, and bronchioles from a terminal bronchiole.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says each segment is divided into lobules, each with a lymphatic, an arteriole, a venule and bronchioles from a terminal bronchiole. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The respiratory system and the ___________________ system equally share the responsibility of supplying oxygen to, and eliminating carbon dioxide from, the body’s cells.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the respiratory and cardiovascular systems share the responsibility of supplying oxygen and eliminating carbon dioxide. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The common cold is a contagious infection of the upper respiratory tract caused by a form of the _____________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the common cold is caused by a form of the rhinovirus. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: As the domelike diaphragm contracts, it moves ____________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the dome-shaped diaphragm moves downward and flattens as it contracts. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: Goblet cells located in the trachea produce ________________________. .
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the goblet cells of the trachea produce mucus. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The oropharynx, has only one opening, the ______________________, which connects with the mouth.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the oropharynx has only one opening, the fauces, which connects with the mouth. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: In the lungs, surfactant is secreted by ___________________ cells.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says surfactant is secreted by certain alveolar cells (type II pneumocytes). Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: Physicians who specialize in the diagnosis and treatment of diseases of the lung are called ________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says pulmonologists are physicians who specialize in diseases of the lungs. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: Tension on the true vocal cords controls ________________________..
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says pitch is controlled by tension on the true vocal cords. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The sense of smell detects ________________________ stimuli.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the nose detects olfactory stimuli for the sense of smell. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The three unpaired pieces of cartilage in the larynx are the thyroid cartilage, the ________________________, and the cricoid cartilage.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 names the three unpaired cartilages as the thyroid cartilage, the epiglottis and the cricoid cartilage. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The paired, rod-shaped ________________________ cartilages are located in the mucous membrane fold that connects the epiglottis to the arytenoid cartilages.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the rod-shaped cuneiform cartilages are in the fold connecting the epiglottis to the arytenoid cartilages. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The pharynx connects to the trachea via the ________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the larynx is a short passageway that connects the pharynx with the trachea. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The anterior portions of the nasal cavities just inside the nostrils are known as the _________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the front portions of the nasal cavities just inside the nostrils are the vestibules. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: Alveolar ducts are also called _______________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says respiratory bronchioles subdivide into alveolar ducts, or atria. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The secretory cells of the lungs are affected in patients with _______________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says cystic fibrosis affects the secretory cells of the lungs. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: Terminal bronchioles subdivide into microscopic branches called ________________________ bronchioles.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says terminal bronchioles subdivide into microscopic branches called respiratory bronchioles. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: On entering the lungs, the primary bronchi divide to form smaller bronchi called _______________ bronchi.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the primary bronchi divide into secondary or lobar bronchi, one for each lobe. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: Air coming from the lungs causes the vocal cords to vibrate and produce sound.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says air from the lungs makes the vocal cords vibrate and produce sound. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The trachea is a passageway for both air and food.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. The trachea carries only air. The pharynx is the shared passage for air and food. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: Cystic fibrosis is caused by excessive exposure to asbestos, silica, or coal dust.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. That describes pneumoconiosis. Cystic fibrosis is inherited. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: Total lung capacity is the maximum volume of air that can be expelled at the normal rate of exhalation after a maximum inspiration.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. That describes vital capacity. Total lung capacity is the volume of gas in the lungs at the end of a maximum inspiration. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.

quiz.q: The epiglottis is a large piece of cartilage that covers the glottis when we swallow.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 17 says the epiglottis is a large leaf-shaped cartilage that forms a lid over the glottis when we swallow. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 17.
